strengths: Defines and studies a timely task: multi-modal controllable joint audio-video generation, with composable conditions including reference image, reference audio, depth, and pose.
Proposes a coherent architecture, MMCU plus a dual-stream bypass, to inject heterogeneous control signals into a frozen joint Diffusion Transformer without disturbing pretrained generative priors.
Introduces modality-specific guidance scaling and a two-stage progressive inference strategy, giving users independent control over visual identity and acoustic timbre at inference time.
Qualitative results and the appendix human evaluation demonstrate plausible control over identity, timbre, pose, and depth, with human raters favoring the method over several baselines.
Training is efficient relative to the backbone size (about 12 hours on 4 H200 GPUs), suggesting the bypass-based adaptation is practical.
weaknesses: No comparison to joint audio-video generation baselines or controlled variants of the same LTX-2 backbone. The paper claims state-of-the-art controllable joint generation, but only compares against audio-driven portrait methods and video-only control methods, which is not sufficient to support the central claim.

Missing ablations for the main technical components: MMCU design, dual-stream bypass, bypass layer placement, projection initialization, and modality-specific guidance scaling. The gamma_v/gamma_a study is qualitative only, so the contribution of each component is unclear.

Audio evaluation is inadequate. The appendix reports only MMControl's own audio metrics, with WER around 17.58% and speaker similarity 0.2574, but no comparison to zero-shot TTS or audio generation baselines. This weakens claims of 'timbre-consistent' and high-quality speech.

The main comparisons are not fully apples-to-apples: baselines use ground-truth first frames and ground-truth audio, while MMControl generates video and speech from text/reference conditions. The reported gains are often marginal or mixed, e.g., Sync-D is not best in Table 1 and aesthetic quality is lower than VACE in Table 2.

Quantitative evaluation is limited: depth control is evaluated only on 200 samples, pose control has no quantitative results, and depth/pose settings lack audio-quality and audio-visual synchronization metrics despite the joint-generation claim. No statistical significance or confidence intervals are provided.

Training data is a 30k subset of Hallo3, which is likely portrait-centric. This limits the evidence for broad scene generation, complex body poses, and general audio-video synthesis. The paper's claims about scene layout and general multi-modal control are therefore overbroad.

Technical novelty is incremental: the core ideas (bypass branches, zero-initialized residual control injection, modality-specific guidance) are close to existing controllable generation adapters such as ControlNet/T2I-Adapter, simply transferred to a joint audio-video DiT.

Reproducibility details are incomplete. The method depends on the LTX-2 19B backbone, but there is no discussion of public availability, code release, training objective/loss details, or dataset licensing, making independent reproduction difficult.

Clarity and attribution issues remain: some citations and table entries are inconsistent, and the paper overclaims 'state-of-the-art' without matching joint-generation baselines or comprehensive ablations.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely gap: controllable generation for joint audio-video diffusion models, where prior work is mostly video-only or audio-only.

The Multi-Modal Control Unit (MMCU) provides a coherent interface for heterogeneous signals such as reference images, reference audio, depth maps, and poses, using temporal concatenation and masks to distinguish reference from generation regions.
The Dual-Stream Bypass design is a plausible engineering solution for injecting modality-specific control into a frozen large joint DiT while preserving pretrained generative priors.
Modality-specific guidance scaling allows independent inference-time adjustment of visual and acoustic control strength, which is practically useful and qualitatively demonstrated.
The paper reports a broad set of evaluations, including VBench-style video metrics, Sync-C/Sync-D, subject DINO, structural depth MAE, and a human study, and also includes an audio quality appendix.
Qualitative examples show composable control over identity, timbre, pose, and depth, and the two-stage progressive inference strategy is a reasonable efficiency-oriented design.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is limited: the core components are essentially ControlNet/adapter-style bypass branches, channel concatenation with masks, and simple scaling of injected hints. The paper does not introduce a substantially new generative mechanism or training objective.

The experimental comparisons are not apples-to-apples. Baselines are video-only or audio-driven methods, often using ground-truth audio and/or the first frame, while MMControl jointly generates audio and video from text. The paper does not compare against a controllable joint audio-video generation baseline or an adapted ControlNet-style baseline for the same joint setting.

There is no quantitative ablation of the proposed components, e.g., MMCU design, visual/acoustic bypass branches, mask channel, zero-initialized output projectors, modality-specific scaling, or the two-stage inference strategy. The decoupled-control study is only qualitative.

Audio evaluation is insufficient for the claims. Audio quality is relegated to the appendix with only absolute metrics, no comparison to TTS or audio generation baselines, and the reported WER (weighted 7.96%, SeedTTS avg 17.58%) and speaker similarity (SIM-o 0.2574) raise concerns about speech fidelity and timbre preservation.

The scope of control is overstated. Acoustic control is essentially reference timbre conditioning; there is no control over pitch, energy, emotion, or other acoustic structure. Visual structural control is evaluated mainly on depth and qualitatively on pose, and pose lacks quantitative structural metrics.

Training and evaluation are limited to a 30k subset of the Hallo3 dataset, which is portrait/talking-head oriented. This does not support broad claims about general joint audio-video generation, scene layout control, or diverse real-world audio-visual scenes.

Reproducibility is weak: the method depends on the proprietary LTX-2 19B backbone and Hallo3 data, with no released code, model, or benchmark. Critical details are missing, including the audio VAE, text encoder, joint audio-video backbone alignment, training objective, upsampler architecture, and how the frozen distilled LoRA is integrated.

The structural depth results are not decisive: MAE improves only modestly over VACE (5.35 to 4.52), while aesthetic quality is actually lower than VACE, and no statistical significance or confidence intervals are provided.

The state-of-the-art claim is based on a self-constructed 200-sample benchmark rather than a public standardized benchmark, and the comparisons do not isolate the effect of joint audio-video generation from the effect of the much larger LTX-2 backbone.

Human evaluation is underpowered and lacks statistical analysis: 20 participants, 5 data points per method, no confidence intervals, and no reported protocol for rater consistency or significance testing.
There are clarity and citation issues, e.g., inconsistent naming such as UniPortrait vs. AniPortrait and Hallo3 citation inconsistencies, which make it harder to verify baselines and claims.
The paper lacks a meaningful limitations and societal-impact discussion, despite operating in a space with clear risks around identity cloning, voice cloning, and deepfake generation.

strengths: Addresses a timely and underexplored problem: fine-grained multi-modal control for native joint audio-video generation, including identity, timbre, depth, and pose conditioning.
The Multi-Modal Control Unit (MMCU) offers a unified, flexible interface for heterogeneous control signals and uses masks to distinguish reference content from generation-time constraints.

The Dual-Stream Bypass architecture injects modality-specific hints into a frozen joint DiT via zero-initialized residual connections, preserving pretrained generative priors and enabling relatively efficient training.
Modality-Specific Guidance Scaling allows independent inference-time adjustment of visual and acoustic control strengths, with a clear qualitative demonstration of decoupled control.

Extensive qualitative results, human evaluation, and additional audio-quality metrics are provided, showing improvements in visual fidelity, identity preservation, lip sync, and structural adherence over several baselines.
The paper is well organized and clearly written, with sufficient implementation details to understand the training pipeline and inference strategy.
weaknesses: Missing quantitative ablations: there is no systematic study isolating the MMCU, dual-stream bypass, mask design, layer placement, zero initialization, modality-specific guidance scaling, or the two-stage inference pipeline, so the contribution of each component is not rigorously established.

The comparison protocol is not fully apples-to-apples. Audio-driven baselines use ground-truth audio and the first frame, while MMControl jointly generates audio and video from text/reference conditions; Sync-C for MMControl is computed against its own generated audio and is not directly comparable to baselines synced to GT audio.

No direct comparison to existing controllable joint audio-video generation methods is provided. The baselines are primarily video-only or audio-driven portrait methods, so the claim of state-of-the-art controllable joint generation is not demonstrated.

Training is limited to 30k samples from Hallo3, which likely biases the model toward portrait/talking-head scenarios. Generalization to open-domain scenes, multiple characters, non-speech audio, complex camera motion, and long-form content is not evaluated.

Pose control is evaluated only qualitatively with no keypoint or pose-error metric, while depth control uses a single MAE metric on only 200 samples. More structural-fidelity metrics and larger benchmarks are needed.

Audio quality results in the appendix are modest or weak (e.g., SIM-o 0.2574, WER 17.58% SeedTTS average) and are not compared against baselines or strong TTS systems, raising questions about generated speech content and timbre fidelity.

The paper does not report variance, confidence intervals, or statistical significance for the quantitative comparisons, and the human study lacks details on inter-rater agreement, randomization, and participant demographics.

The two-stage progressive inference depends on a frozen distilled LoRA from LTX-2, but its effect on control fidelity, audio quality, and cross-modal alignment is not ablated. It is also unclear how much Stage 2 improves over a single-stage baseline.

The reference-image protocol is ambiguous: if the reference image is the ground-truth first frame of the target video, identity preservation is partly reconstruction rather than customization; if it is a separate image, the training/reference construction and leakage controls should be clarified.
Reproducibility is a concern due to reliance on the LTX-2 19B backbone and unclear availability of code, model weights, and the curated Hallo3 subset, making independent verification difficult.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored gap: unified multi-modal control for native joint audio-video generation. The task formulation and MMCU provide a simple interface for heterogeneous controls, including reference image, reference audio, depth, and pose.

The Dual-Stream Bypass design is a reasonable way to add controllable branches while freezing a large pretrained joint DiT, and modality-specific guidance scaling gives users independent inference-time control over visual and acoustic conditions.

Experiments are extensive for an applied/algorithms contribution: multiple control settings, quantitative metrics, qualitative comparisons, a user study, audio quality evaluation, component/guidance ablations, and a comparison with a concurrent AVControl method.

Structural control results are promising: depth and pose MAE improve over the compared baselines, and the ablations support the usefulness of the MMCU masks, projector weight inheritance, dual-stream branches, and the decision to omit explicit AV cross-attention inside bypass branches.
weaknesses: Evaluation is narrow: training uses 30k Hallo3 samples, which are portrait/talking-head-centric, and the constructed benchmark remains in this domain. Claims about broad 'scene structure' and general multi-modal control are not sufficiently validated on open-domain scenes, multi-character conversations, or long videos.

Joint-control evaluation is incomplete: the depth and pose tables report only visual/structural metrics and omit audio synchronization, timbre consistency, or audio quality under structural controls. The audio-driven comparison also uses GT audio/first frame for baselines while MMControl generates speech from text, which does not cleanly isolate the contribution of reference-audio timbre control.

Direct joint audio-video controllable baselines are missing. The video-only baselines used for depth/pose do not generate audio, and the audio-driven baselines are not joint AV generators, so it is difficult to assess how much of the gain comes from the proposed control mechanism versus the stronger LTX-2 backbone.

Reproducibility is questionable: the method depends on LTX-2 19B, a curated Hallo3 subset, and a constructed evaluation set whose availability is unclear. Key training details, such as the loss formulation, modality-dropout schedule, and handling of combined conditions, are not sufficiently specified.

Several technical details are ambiguous: how visual and acoustic hints are combined in the main transformer block, what mask values are used for empty structural controls, and how the acoustic bypass learns timbre identity from concatenated reference/silence latents without an explicit speaker embedding.

The 'state-of-the-art' claim is stronger than the evidence warrants. Gains on several visual metrics are marginal, with worse Dynamic Degree and Sync-D than Hallo3 in Table 1 and worse Aesthetic Quality than VACE in depth control, and no statistical significance or error bars are reported for the small benchmark/user-study sets.

Audio quality evidence is limited: the reported speaker similarity (SIM-o 0.2574) and SeedTTS average WER (17.58%) are not particularly strong, and there is no comparison to dedicated TTS or audio generation baselines under the reference-timbre setting.
The paper lacks discussion of misuse risks for identity- and voice-controllable audio-video generation, which is a meaningful omission for this application area.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant and challenging problem: unified multi-modal control in joint audio-video generation, with composable reference image/audio, depth, and pose conditions.

The proposed Multi-Modal Control Unit and dual-stream bypass architecture are reasonably described, and the ablation studies suggest that several components, especially projector inheritance and modality-specific bypass branches, contribute to performance.
The paper reports multiple evaluations (sync, identity, depth/pose MAE, human study, audio metrics) and qualitative examples, showing some promise for the approach.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the core ideas are adapter/ControlNet-style bypass branches, masked token concatenation, and inference-time guidance scaling; the two-stage progressive inference and several components are inherited from LTX-2 rather than introduced.

The evaluation is not a convincing validation of the claimed state-of-the-art in joint controllable audio-video generation. Main audio-driven baselines (SadTalker, AniPortrait, Hallo3) are not joint audio-video generators and use ground-truth audio/first frame in a different setting, while MMControl jointly generates audio; this makes audio-visual synchronization comparisons apples-to-oranges.

There is no direct comparison to a controllable joint audio-video generation baseline on audio/timbre control; the only AVControl comparison is in the appendix and covers depth/pose only, so the central claim of unified audio-video control is under-supported.

The experiments are limited to 200/150-sample in-house splits from a Hallo3 subset, with no standard benchmark protocol, no statistical significance testing, and little reporting of variance or failure cases.

Reproducibility is weak: architecture dimensions, audio-video VAE details, number of bypass blocks, inference cost, data splits, and training/inference hyperparameters are insufficiently specified, and no code/model release is mentioned.

Several quantitative comparisons are questionable: metrics such as Sync-C on self-generated audio versus GT-audio baselines, depth/pose MAE after re-extracting structure from generated videos, and inconsistent improvements across metrics do not establish clear superiority.

The human and audio evaluations are underpowered and incomplete: only 20 participants rating a few samples, no audio baselines, low speaker similarity (SIM-o 0.2574), and no comparison to strong TTS/voice-cloning methods.

The manuscript has clarity and presentation issues (e.g., table typos such as 'Halls3', 'Halled', 'SurTaller', inconsistent method names), overclaims of state-of-the-art, and no explicit limitations or societal-impact discussion.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: unified multi-modal control for joint audio-video generation, moving beyond visual-only controllable generation.

The Multi-Modal Control Unit (MMCU) is a sensible interface for heterogeneous controls (reference image/audio, depth, pose), using masks to distinguish reference content from generation frames and enabling composable control.

The Dual-Stream Bypass design is a reasonable way to inject modality-specific control into a frozen joint DiT while preserving pretrained generative priors; zero-initialized output projection and inherited projector weights are standard but effective training-stability choices.
Modality-specific guidance scaling is a useful and practical inference-time mechanism for independently adjusting visual identity and acoustic timbre strength, supported by a decoupled-control study.

The two-stage progressive inference strategy is well motivated for high-resolution refinement and computational efficiency, and the overall training cost (7,200 steps on 4 H200s) is modest for a 19B backbone.

The experimental suite covers multiple control settings (audio-driven/reference, depth, pose) and reports a broad set of metrics including sync, identity, text alignment, structure error, and human evaluation.
Ablations in the appendix provide useful evidence for MMCU masks, projector weight inheritance, dual-stream design, and the choice to omit bypass audio-video cross-attention.
Qualitative results demonstrate plausible identity-, timbre-, pose-, and depth-controlled joint generation, and the writing is generally clear and well organized.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is largely integrative: ControlNet-style bypass branches, adapters, and guidance scaling are adapted to a joint audio-video DiT. This is acceptable for a systems contribution, but the paper should calibrate novelty claims accordingly.

The main comparisons are not fully apples-to-apples: audio-driven baselines use ground-truth audio and first frames while MMControl jointly generates speech and video; depth/pose baselines are video-only and cannot generate audio. This complicates claims of superiority in joint audio-video generation.

There is no direct comparison against existing joint audio-video controllable generation frameworks on the same task, which weakens the stated state-of-the-art claim for controllable joint generation.

Audio quality evidence is limited: only self-reported SIM-o, UTMOS, and WER are provided, with no comparison to audio generation or voice cloning baselines and no human listening study. SIM-o 0.2574 and SeedTTS average WER 17.58% are not strongly convincing on their own.

Generalization is under-demonstrated: training and evaluation rely on a 30k subset of Hallo3, which is largely portrait/talking-head focused. Claims about depth-guided scene structure and broad motion control are not sufficiently supported across diverse domains, scenes, or multi-character settings.

Evaluation scale is modest (200 samples in main comparisons, 90 for ablations, 60 for AVControl) and lacks confidence intervals or statistical significance tests. The human study details are thin, with no inter-rater agreement or participant/variance analysis.

Some metrics may be unreliable: depth/pose MAE from re-extracted signals can be sensitive to alignment/scale/occlusion; Dynamic Degree measures motion magnitude but not motion quality; Text CLIP over eight frames may miss temporal semantic alignment.

Reproducibility is uncertain: the method depends on LTX-2 19B and other large pretrained components, and key details for the bypass projectors, mask channel initialization, and Stage 2 MMCU re-encoding are incomplete. No code or model release is stated.
The paper does not discuss misuse risks of identity- and voice-controllable audio-video generation (e.g., deepfakes, voice cloning, consent), which is a meaningful omission for this application area.

There are minor clarity/notation issues: Eq. 5 suggests a single modality residual per block although both visual and acoustic streams are active, and some terminology/reference inconsistencies appear in tables and citations.
